meta.description: Sherlock Holmes never says it. The phrase is in none of Conan Doyle's 60 stories — its earliest known exact match is an 1908 London newspaper joke.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Elementary, my dear Watson'?
meta.ogDescription: Conan Doyle never wrote it. The earliest exact match is a courtroom joke in The Globe, London, 27 February 1908 — and the coiner is still unknown.

answer.label: Not Arthur Conan Doyle — a line his readers wrote for him
answer.authorDates: Coiner unidentified · earliest exact match in print: February 1908
answer.sourceLine: The phrase appears nowhere in Arthur Conan Doyle’s sixty Sherlock Holmes tales. It is a folk coinage — assembled by readers out of two things Holmes really does say — and Quote Investigator reports that the identity of whoever first put the four words together remains unknown. The earliest documented exact match is a courtroom joke in The Globe and Traveller (London), 27 February 1908.

source.excerpt:
“I see that you are professionally rather busy just now,” said he, glancing very keenly across at me.

“Yes, I’ve had a busy day,” I answered. “It may seem very foolish in your eyes,” I added, “but really I don’t know how you deduced it.”

Holmes chuckled to himself.

“I have the advantage of knowing your habits, my dear Watson,” said he. “When your round is a short one you walk, and when it is a long one you use a hansom. As I perceive that your boots, although used, are by no means dirty, I cannot doubt that you are at present busy enough to justify the hansom.”

“Excellent!” I cried.

“Elementary,” said he.
trail: 1893 — Doyle gets close, and stops. In “The Adventure of the Crooked Man” ↗ Holmes calls his friend “my dear Watson” — then, a paragraph later, answers Watson’s “Excellent!” with one word: “Elementary.” Every ingredient is on the page; the sentence is not.

1901 — the joke is already running. A parody in the Northampton Mercury has a Holmes figure say “Elementary, my dear Potson” (Word Histories ↗). You cannot parody a catchphrase that does not yet exist — so by 1901 the pattern was already in the public ear.

1908 — the earliest exact match. A courtroom squib in The Globe and Traveller (London) of 27 February 1908 runs: “‘My dear Holmes,’ I cried, astonished, ‘how——?’ ‘Elementary, my dear Watson,’ he replied carelessly” (Word Histories ↗). Not a Holmes story — a newspaper gag about a barrister.

1929 — Hollywood makes it official. The line is spoken at the very end of The Return of Sherlock Holmes, the first Holmes sound film (Wikiquote ↗). It is the moment the phrase became unshakeable — and it is still not the moment it was born.
source.cutTag: The Adventure of the Crooked Man (1893)
source.excerptNote: Both halves of the famous phrase are here — and they are a paragraph apart, in the wrong order, as Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ points out. Read it once and you can feel the mistake being made: the memory tidies the two lines into one, and the tidied version is the one the world kept.

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted here, because the wording has no identified author: the phrase is in none of Conan Doyle’s stories, and Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the identity of its coiner remains uncertain. The documented texts quoted on this page — Doyle’s “The Adventure of the Crooked Man” (1893), the 1908 Globe item, and Wodehouse’s Psmith, Journalist — were all published well before 1931 and are public domain in the United States, but that status attaches to those works, not to this orphan phrase.

author.heading: About Arthur Conan Doyle
author.metaLine: 1859–1930 · British physician and writer · creator of Sherlock Holmes
author.bio: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 – 7 July 1930) was a British writer and physician, knighted in 1902, who wrote four novels and fifty-six short stories about Sherlock Holmes. He gave Holmes the word “Elementary” and gave him the habit of calling Watson “my dear Watson” — but he never once joined them into a sentence. The most famous line his character ever “said” is one he never wrote, which makes it less a forgery than a collaboration between an author and a century of readers.

cite.sourceCitation: No canonical source: the phrase appears in none of Arthur Conan Doyle’s sixty Sherlock Holmes stories. Closest canonical wording: Arthur Conan Doyle, “The Adventure of the Crooked Man,” in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes (1893).

misattribution.heading: The most famous thing he never wrote
misattribution.intro: This is the rare misquotation with no villain. Four suspects are routinely named as the source, and the evidence clears all four — including the man whose character says it.

items.why: The complete phrase appears in none of the sixty Holmes tales, as both Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ establish. A full-text search of all nine canonical volumes at Project Gutenberg confirms it: zero matches. The parts are his; the sentence is not.

items.who: The 1929 film The Return of Sherlock Holmes
items.why: The line is spoken at the very end of the first Sherlock Holmes sound film (Wikiquote ↗), and the internet routinely credits it as the birthplace. But the phrase was already in print in 1908 ↗ — two decades before the film could say a word out loud.

Psmith really does murmur “Elementary, my dear Watson, elementary ↗” in Psmith, Journalist, and the line is sometimes called its first recorded use. It is not: the newspaper citations run earlier, and Wodehouse is making a joke that depends on his readers already knowing the phrase.

The actor’s 1899 stage Holmes is the standing Sherlockian hypothesis, argued at I Hear of Sherlock Everywhere ↗ — which itself concedes the point is speculative, since audiences may simply have blended two phrases they already knew. The play text ↗ has Holmes tell Watson only: “Elementary! The child’s play of deduction!”

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who said it first. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the exact wording no further back than a courtroom squib in The Globe of February 1908 and concludes that the identity of the coiner remains uncertain — the line was assembled by readers out of Doyle’s own parts, then handed back to his detective.

context.heading: How a quote gets written by its readers
lead: Most fake quotes are a theft: someone’s words pinned on a more famous name. This one is stranger. Nobody stole anything — readers simply built the sentence themselves out of parts Conan Doyle left lying around, and handed it back to his character. Holmes says “Elementary.” Holmes says “my dear Watson.” The mind closes the gap, and the memory of the line becomes more vivid than any line on the page.

By the time the phrase first surfaces in print in 1908, it is already being used as a punchline — which means the joke was old before it was ever written down. You cannot make a gag out of a catchphrase nobody recognises. The written record catches the phrase mid-flight, long after it had entered the spoken language, and that is precisely why its author cannot be found: it never had one.
context.detailsSummary: The suspects, and why none of them convict
detailsBody: The 1929 film. The usual culprit named online is The Return of Sherlock Holmes, the first Sherlock Holmes sound film, which ends with the line. It is a popularizer, not a source: the phrase was in print by 1908, twenty-one years earlier.

P. G. Wodehouse. Psmith murmurs “Elementary, my dear Watson, elementary” in Psmith, Journalist — a genuine early appearance, and one you can read for yourself. But it is a joke told at the reader’s expense, and it only lands if the reader already knows the line. Wodehouse is quoting the street, not inventing the phrase.

William Gillette. Sherlockians have long suspected the actor whose 1899 stage Holmes defined the character for a generation. It is a real hypothesis and it is unproven. The text of the play has Holmes say to Watson only: “Elementary! The child’s play of deduction!” The theory is that years of performance, and audiences blending two familiar phrases, did the rest — which, if true, is not an origin so much as a description of the same collective process.
context.pull: “Elementary,” said he. That is as close as Conan Doyle ever came.
